title: 18 — Python & Data Engineering
html:
18 — Python & Data Engineering

Scope: CPython's execution and memory model, modern tooling, and the dataframe/analytics stack — with Polars treated as the primary engine and pandas as the incumbent you interoperate with.

1. CPython: the model underneath

1.1 Everything is an object

name ──▶ PyObject
          ├── refcount
          ├── type pointer
          └── value
  • Names are bindings, not boxes. a = b makes both names point to the same object; it never copies.
  • Mutable vs immutable is the whole story. int, str, tuple, frozenset are immutable; list, dict, set, and most objects are mutable.
  • Memory: reference counting (immediate deallocation at refcount 0) plus a generational cycle collector for reference cycles. sys.getrefcount, gc module.
  • Small-object caches: ints −5..256 and short interned strings are shared singletons — which is why a is b sometimes surprises you. Use == for equality; is only for None/sentinels.
# The two classic Python gotchas, both explained by mutability + binding
def append(item, target=[]):        # ❌ default evaluated ONCE at def time
    target.append(item)
    return target
append(1); append(2)                # [1, 2] — shared across calls

def append(item, target: list | None = None) -> list:   # ✔
    target = [] if target is None else target
    target.append(item)
    return target

rows = [{"a": 1}] * 3               # ❌ three references to the SAME dict
rows = [{"a": 1} for _ in range(3)] # ✔ three distinct dicts

1.2 The GIL and what to do about it

Covered in file 12 §7. The one-line rule:

Threads for I/O, processes for pure-Python CPU work, native libraries (NumPy/Polars/DuckDB) for data-parallel CPU work — and the last one is almost always the right answer.

1.3 Performance characteristics

Operation Cost Note
Attribute access ~30 ns Dict lookup; local variables are much faster
Function call ~50–100 ns Python calls are expensive relative to the work in tight loops
list.append amortised O(1)
list.pop(0) / list.insert(0,x) O(n) Use collections.deque
x in list O(n) Use a set — this is the #1 accidental O(n²) in Python
dict/set lookup O(1)
String concatenation in a loop O(n²) Use "".join(parts) 
# The single most common accidental quadratic in data code
valid_ids = load_ids()               # a list of 100_000
rows = [r for r in data if r.id in valid_ids]     # ❌ 100k × 100k comparisons

valid_ids = set(load_ids())          # ✔ O(1) membership → linear overall

Optimisation order: better algorithm/data structure → vectorise with a native library → cache → functools.lru_cache → C extension/Cython/Rust → parallelise. Profile first (cProfile + snakeviz, py-spy top --pid for a live process, line_profiler for line-level, memray/tracemalloc for memory).

2. Modern Python practice

2.1 Tooling

Concern Tool Command
Env + deps + Python versions uv uv init, uv add polars, uv run app.py, uv sync
Lint + format ruff ruff check --fix ., ruff format .
Types mypy or pyright mypy src/
Tests pytest pytest -q --cov=src
Task runner make / just / uv run scripts
Pre-commit pre-commit ruff, mypy, gitleaks, trailing whitespace 
# pyproject.toml — one file for everything
[project]
name = "overlap-engine"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = ["polars>=1.0", "pydantic>=2.7", "httpx>=0.27"]

[dependency-groups]
dev = ["pytest>=8", "pytest-cov", "mypy", "ruff"]

[tool.ruff]
line-length = 100
[tool.ruff.lint]
select = ["E", "F", "I", "N", "UP", "B", "SIM", "RUF", "ANN", "PTH", "C4"]

[tool.mypy]
strict = true
warn_unreachable = true

2.2 Typing and data modelling

from dataclasses import dataclass
from decimal import Decimal
from typing import Protocol, Self

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)          # immutable + memory-efficient
class Holding:
    instrument: str
    weight: Decimal
    market_value: Decimal

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        if not (0 <= self.weight <= 1):
            raise ValueError(f"weight must be in [0, 1], got {self.weight}")

class PriceSource(Protocol):                  # structural typing — no inheritance needed
    def price(self, instrument: str) -> Decimal: ...
Use For
@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True) Internal value objects — fast, no external dependency
pydantic v2 Anything crossing a boundary: API payloads, config, external files. Validation + coercion + JSON schema
TypedDict Typing a dict shape you can't change (legacy JSON)
Protocol Duck-typed interfaces without inheritance
Enum / StrEnum Closed sets of values

⚠️ Never pass raw dicts across module boundaries. They have no contract, no validation, no IDE support, and every consumer re-implements the same .get("field", default) defensive code.

⚠️ Decimal for money, always. 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 in binary floating point; financial sums drift. Set the context precision explicitly.

2.3 Errors, resources, logging

import logging
from pathlib import Path

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)          # module-level, never the root logger

class PricingError(Exception):
    """Raised when a price cannot be determined for an instrument."""

def load_prices(path: Path) -> dict[str, Decimal]:
    try:
        with path.open(encoding="utf-8") as handle:      # context manager: always closed
            return parse(handle)
    except FileNotFoundError as exc:
        raise PricingError(f"Price file not found: {path}") from exc   # chain the cause
    except ValueError as exc:
        logger.warning("Malformed price file %s: %s", path, exc)
        raise PricingError(f"Price file {path} is malformed") from exc

Rules: no bare except:; catch specific exceptions; always raise ... from exc; pathlib.Path over os.path; logging with lazy %s formatting (not f-strings — they're evaluated even when the level is disabled) and never print in library code.

3. Polars

3.1 Why it's different

pandas Polars
Engine NumPy/Python, single-threaded Rust, multi-threaded, Apache Arrow memory
Execution Eager only Eager and lazy (query optimiser)
Index Yes (a frequent source of bugs) No index — explicit joins only
Nulls NaN/None/NaT inconsistency One unified null
Strings Python objects Arrow UTF-8
Memory Often 2–5× the data size Closer to data size, zero-copy where possible
Larger than RAM ✘ ✔ streaming engine
Typical speed baseline 5–30× on multi-core aggregations/joins

3.2 Expressions — the core idea

A Polars expression is a description of a computation, not a value. The engine can parallelise, reorder, and fuse expressions.

import polars as pl

result = (
    df
    .filter(pl.col("trade_date").is_between(start, end))
    .with_columns(
        notional_gbp = pl.col("notional") * pl.col("fx_rate"),
        is_large     = pl.col("notional") > 1_000_000,
        year_month   = pl.col("trade_date").dt.strftime("%Y-%m"),
    )
    .group_by("portfolio_id", "year_month")
    .agg(
        total     = pl.col("notional_gbp").sum(),
        trades    = pl.len(),
        largest   = pl.col("notional_gbp").max(),
        avg_large = pl.col("notional_gbp").filter(pl.col("is_large")).mean(),
    )
    .sort("portfolio_id", "year_month")
)

Every expression in with_columns/agg runs in parallel across threads. That's the performance model in one sentence.

3.3 Lazy evaluation — the real win

lazy = (
    pl.scan_parquet("data/trades/*.parquet")        # scan_*, not read_* → nothing loaded yet
      .filter(pl.col("trade_date") >= start)        # pushed down into the Parquet reader
      .select(["portfolio_id", "instrument", "notional"])   # projection pushdown: fewer columns read
      .join(pl.scan_parquet("data/instruments.parquet"), on="instrument", how="inner")
      .group_by("portfolio_id")
      .agg(pl.col("notional").sum())
)

print(lazy.explain())                # inspect the optimised plan — do this when tuning
df = lazy.collect()                  # optimise + execute
df = lazy.collect(engine="streaming")  # process in batches; handles larger-than-RAM

What the optimiser does: predicate pushdown (filter at the file/row-group level), projection pushdown (read only needed columns), common subexpression elimination, slice pushdown, join reordering, and type coercion. On columnar files, pushdown routinely cuts I/O by 90%+.

3.4 Idioms and traps

# ✔ Chain; each step is a new lazy/eager frame — no mutation, no SettingWithCopyWarning equivalent
# ✔ Use expressions, never Python loops over rows
df.with_columns(score = pl.col("a") * 0.6 + pl.col("b") * 0.4)

# ❌ Row-wise Python — kills every advantage (single-threaded, per-row interpreter overhead)
df.with_columns(score = pl.struct(["a","b"]).map_elements(lambda r: r["a"]*0.6 + r["b"]*0.4))

# Conditional logic stays vectorised
df.with_columns(
    band = pl.when(pl.col("notional") > 1e6).then(pl.lit("large"))
            .when(pl.col("notional") > 1e5).then(pl.lit("medium"))
            .otherwise(pl.lit("small"))
)

# Window functions without a group_by collapse
df.with_columns(
    pct_of_portfolio = pl.col("market_value") / pl.col("market_value").sum().over("portfolio_id")
)

# Joins: validate cardinality so a silent fan-out doesn't multiply your rows
merged = trades.join(instruments, on="instrument", how="left", validate="m:1")

# Explicit schema on read — avoids inference cost and surprise type changes between files
df = pl.read_csv(path, schema_overrides={"notional": pl.Float64, "trade_date": pl.Date})

⚠️ Traps:

  • map_elements / apply is an escape hatch to Python — treat every use as a performance bug to justify.
  • Joins without validate= silently duplicate rows when the right side isn't unique. This is the most common data-correctness bug in dataframe pipelines.
  • float for money — use Decimal at the boundaries or integer minor units, and be explicit about rounding.
  • Nulls propagate through arithmetic; sum() skips them but + doesn't. Decide null handling per column.
  • Reading many small files is slow — consolidate into larger Parquet row groups (target ~128 MB files).

3.5 Interop

arrow_table = df.to_arrow()          # zero-copy
pandas_df   = df.to_pandas(use_pyarrow_extension_array=True)
df          = pl.from_pandas(pandas_df)
numpy_arr   = df["notional"].to_numpy()

# DuckDB reads Polars/Arrow directly — use SQL where SQL is clearer
import duckdb
out = duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT portfolio_id, sum(notional) AS total
    FROM df
    WHERE trade_date >= '2026-01-01'
    GROUP BY portfolio_id
""").pl()

Polars + DuckDB is a strong local analytics stack: Polars for expression pipelines, DuckDB for complex SQL (window functions, recursive CTEs, multi-way joins), Arrow as the zero-copy bridge between them.

3.6 .NET ↔ Python interop (relevant to your stack)

Options, roughly in order of operational simplicity:

Approach Latency Isolation Notes
Parquet/Arrow files on shared storage Batch Full Simplest, most debuggable; ideal for scheduled jobs
HTTP/gRPC microservice (FastAPI) ms Full Independent scaling and deployment; standard choice
Message queue async Full Long-running jobs, retries, backpressure
CSnakes / Python.NET (in-process) µs None Fastest, but a Python crash takes the host down; GIL contention; deployment couples the runtimes
Subprocess + stdin/stdout ms Process Crude but robust for CLI-shaped work

Recommendation: in-process embedding only when latency genuinely demands it. Otherwise a small FastAPI service or Arrow files on disk gives you independent deploys, independent failure, and a much simpler debugging story.

4. Data pipeline engineering

4.1 Architecture

flowchart LR
    S1[(Operational DB)] -->|CDC / batch extract| L[Landing / raw<br/>immutable, as-received]
    S2[Files / SFTP] --> L
    S3[APIs] --> L
    L --> B[Bronze: raw + metadata<br/>Parquet, partitioned by date]
    B --> SI[Silver: cleaned, typed,<br/>deduplicated, conformed]
    SI --> G[Gold: business aggregates,<br/>marts, feature tables]
    G --> C[Consumers: BI, API, ML, reports]
    V[Data quality checks] -.gate.-> SI
    V -.gate.-> G

The medallion (bronze/silver/gold) pattern exists because of one rule: never overwrite the raw data. If a transformation is wrong, you must be able to reprocess from the original bytes. Landing/bronze is append-only and immutable.

4.2 Non-negotiable properties

Property How
Idempotent Re-running for the same partition produces the same result. Use overwrite-partition or merge-on-key, never blind append
Partitioned By date (usually) — enables incremental processing, cheap backfills, and pruning
Incremental Process only the new/changed partition; a full reload should be possible but not routine
Replayable Backfill any historical window with one parameterised command
Observable Row counts in/out, null rates, duration, schema hash, freshness — logged per run
Validated Contract checks at each boundary; fail the run, don't publish bad data
Lineage Which inputs produced this output, with what code version 
def run_partition(as_of: date, *, dry_run: bool = False) -> RunResult:
    """Idempotent: safe to re-run for the same as_of date."""
    raw = pl.scan_parquet(f"bronze/trades/dt={as_of:%Y-%m-%d}/*.parquet")

    cleaned = (
        raw.filter(pl.col("notional").is_not_null() & (pl.col("notional") > 0))
           .unique(subset=["trade_id"], keep="last")          # explicit dedupe policy
           .with_columns(pl.col("trade_date").cast(pl.Date))
    )

    frame = cleaned.collect(engine="streaming")
    validate(frame, expectations=TRADE_EXPECTATIONS)          # raises on breach

    if not dry_run:
        target = Path(f"silver/trades/dt={as_of:%Y-%m-%d}")
        write_atomic(frame, target)      # write to .tmp, then atomic rename — no partial reads

    return RunResult(as_of=as_of, rows_in=raw.select(pl.len()).collect().item(),
                     rows_out=frame.height)

4.3 Data quality

TRADE_EXPECTATIONS = [
    Expectation("no_nulls_in_key",   lambda df: df["trade_id"].null_count() == 0),
    Expectation("weights_sum_to_1",  lambda df: abs(df["weight"].sum() - 1.0) < 1e-6),
    Expectation("no_future_dates",   lambda df: df["trade_date"].max() <= date.today()),
    Expectation("row_count_sane",    lambda df: 0.5 * expected <= df.height <= 1.5 * expected),
]

Categories worth checking every run: schema (columns, types), completeness (null rates, row counts vs the historical range), uniqueness (key duplicates), referential (orphan foreign keys), range/domain (values in valid sets), freshness (max timestamp within SLA), reconciliation (totals match the source system).

⚠️ Fail loudly and stop. Publishing subtly wrong numbers is worse than publishing nothing — downstream decisions get made on them, and the damage is discovered weeks later. Quarantine bad rows, alert, and hold the previous good version.

4.4 File formats

Format Use Note
Parquet The default for analytics Columnar, compressed, typed, predicate/projection pushdown, splittable
Arrow/Feather In-memory and IPC Zero-copy between processes/languages
Delta / Iceberg Table format over Parquet ACID, time travel, schema evolution, concurrent writers
CSV Interchange only No types, no compression, ambiguous quoting/encoding. Never a storage format
JSON / JSONL Semi-structured landing Verbose; JSONL at least streams
Avro Row-oriented streaming Common in Kafka with a schema registry

Parquet practicalities: target ~128 MB files and ~1M-row row groups; too many small files destroys performance ("small file problem"); sort within partitions on your common filter column to improve row-group pruning; use dictionary encoding for low-cardinality strings.

4.5 Orchestration

Tool Model Use
Airflow Task DAGs, schedule-driven The incumbent; large ecosystem
Dagster Asset-driven, typed, testable Best-in-class developer experience and lineage
Prefect Pythonic flows, dynamic Lightweight
dbt SQL transformations + tests + docs Warehouse-side modelling, pairs with any of the above
Azure Data Factory / Synapse Managed, low-code Azure-native shops
Hangfire / Quartz / k8s CronJob Simple scheduling When you don't need a DAG engine

What orchestration must give you: dependency ordering, retries with backoff, alerting, backfill by parameter, run history, SLA/freshness monitoring, and idempotent task semantics. If your "orchestration" is a chain of cron jobs with no visibility into failures, that's the gap to close first.

4.6 Scale

Data size Tool
< 1 GB pandas, or Polars for the speed
1 GB – 100 GB Polars (streaming) or DuckDB on a single machine. Modern hardware handles far more than people assume
100 GB – 10 TB DuckDB/Polars on a big box, or Spark/Databricks, or a cloud warehouse
> 10 TB Spark / warehouse / lakehouse

⚠️ Distributed processing is a last resort, not a default. A 64-core machine with 512 GB of RAM running DuckDB will beat a small Spark cluster on most workloads under a terabyte, for a fraction of the complexity and cost. Prove you need distribution before you buy its operational overhead.

5. Serving Python from a service

from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

app = FastAPI(title="Overlap Engine", version="1.0.0")

class OverlapRequest(BaseModel):
    portfolio_a: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=32)
    portfolio_b: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=32)
    as_of: date

class OverlapResponse(BaseModel):
    overlap_pct: float
    common_holdings: int
    as_of: date

@app.post("/overlap", response_model=OverlapResponse)
async def compute_overlap(request: OverlapRequest) -> OverlapResponse:
    try:
        result = await run_in_threadpool(engine.compute, request)   # CPU work off the event loop
    except UnknownPortfolioError as exc:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail=str(exc)) from exc
    return OverlapResponse(**result)

Production checklist for a Python service: pydantic validation at the boundary; CPU-bound work moved off the event loop (run_in_threadpool or a process pool); uvicorn/gunicorn with an appropriate worker count; structured JSON logging with correlation IDs; /health endpoints; OpenTelemetry instrumentation; a pinned lockfile in the image; non-root container user; and a request timeout.

6. Checklist & interview angles

Python/data checklist

  • uv for environments; lockfile committed; ruff + mypy in CI
  • Type hints on public functions; pydantic/dataclasses at boundaries — no raw dicts across modules
  • Decimal or integer minor units for money; explicit rounding policy
  • No mutable default arguments; no bare except; exceptions chained with from
  • Context managers for all resources
  • Vectorised expressions, not row loops; map_elements justified where used
  • Joins declare cardinality (validate=)
  • Lazy scans with pushdown for large inputs; explain() checked when tuning
  • Pipelines idempotent, partitioned, incremental, replayable
  • Data quality gates that fail the run; bad rows quarantined
  • Raw/bronze layer immutable; transformations reproducible from it
  • Row counts, null rates, freshness, and duration logged per run
  • Parquet with sensible file sizes; no small-file explosion
  • Profiled before optimising (py-spy, cProfile, memray)

🔍 Interview angles

  • What is the GIL and how do you work around it? One thread executes bytecode at a time; released during I/O and in native extensions. Processes for pure-Python CPU work; native libraries for data-parallel work.
  • Why is Polars faster than pandas? Rust + multithreading + Arrow columnar memory + a lazy query optimiser with predicate/projection pushdown, and no index semantics to preserve.
  • When would you still use pandas? Ecosystem interop (statsmodels, scikit-learn pipelines, plotting), existing code, and small data where it doesn't matter.
  • How do you make a data pipeline idempotent? Deterministic partition keys, overwrite-partition or merge-on-key writes, atomic publish (write-then-rename), and dedupe with an explicit keep policy.
  • How do you handle a schema change from an upstream source? Explicit schema on read, a contract test that fails the run on drift, versioned bronze data so you can reprocess, and additive-only evolution downstream.
  • is vs ==? Identity vs equality; is only for None and sentinels — small-int and string interning make it look correct in tests and fail in production.
  • What's the difference between a list comprehension and a generator? The comprehension materialises everything; the generator yields lazily with constant memory. Use generators for large or streaming data.
  • When is distributed processing justified? When a single large machine genuinely can't hold or process the data in the required window — measure the single-node option first.
